segments.caption: The Monty Hall problem.
The game, the answer that broke the internet, 3 easy ways to see it, and a 1,000-game test. Save this one!
You're on a game show. Three doors. Behind one is a brand new car. Behind the other two: goats.
You pick door number one.
The host, who knows where the car is, opens door number three. A goat.
Now he asks: do you want to switch to door number two? Stick or switch? Comment your answer.
Most people say it doesn't matter. Two doors left, so 50-50.
Wrong. If you switch, you win 2 out of 3 times. Switching doubles your chance.
In 1990, a columnist named Marilyn vos Savant said this, and thousands of readers, including mathematicians, wrote in to say she was wrong. She was right.
Here's the first way to see it.
When you picked door one, you had a 1 in 3 chance of being right. That never changes.
So there's a 2 in 3 chance the car is behind one of the other two doors. The host just opens the goat among them, and the whole 2 in 3 moves onto the last door.
Second way: just list every case.
Car behind door one: switching loses.
Car behind door two: the host opens three, you switch to two, you win.
Car behind door three: the host opens two, you switch to three, you win.
Switching wins in 2 of the 3 cases.
Third way, the one that makes it click. Imagine 100 doors.
You pick one. The host opens 98 goat doors, leaving just your door and one other.
Would you stick with your random pick, or switch to the one door he carefully avoided? Obviously, switch.
Still not convinced? We played 1,000 games on a computer.
Always sticking won 333 cars. Always switching won 667.
The key is the host. He knows where the car is, and he never opens it.
His choice isn't random, so it gives you information. That's why the odds aren't 50-50.
And it's not just game shows. When new information arrives, update your odds. Don't freeze on your first guess.
That's exactly how doctors read test results, how spam filters learn, and how data scientists think. It's called Bayesian thinking.
So remember: always switch. 2 in 3 beats 1 in 3.
Save this, and try it on a friend with three cups and a coin.
Your turn: in the 100-door version, if you switch, what's your chance of winning the car? Vote in the caption poll!
